BEFORE THE

RESPONSE OF ENCHANTED ROCK, LLC 
Enchanted Rock, LLC (“Enchanted Rock”) submits this response (“Response”) in 
connection with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission”)’s February 20, 
2025 “Order Instituting Proceeding under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act and 
Consolidating with Other Proceedings.”1  In the Show Cause Order, the Commission directed 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) and the PJM transmission owners to show cause as to why 
the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff, the Amended and Restated Operating Agreement of 
PJM, and Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities in the PJM Region 
(together, the “Tariff”)2 remains just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or 
preferential, or explain what changes to the Tariff would remedy the identified concerns if the 
Commission were to determine that the Tariff has become unjust and unreasonable or unduly 
discriminatory or preferential and establish a replacement Tariff.3
Enchanted Rock submits this response in accordance with the Commission’s directive in 
the Show Cause Order providing that interested entities may respond within 30 days of the show 
cause filings to address whether the Tariff remains just and reasonable and not unduly 
1 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 (2025) (“Show Cause Order”). 
2 Capitalized terms not otherwise defined herein have the same meaning as in the Tariff. 
3 See Show Cause Order at P 2.

2 
discriminatory or preferential, and if not, what changes to the Tariff should be implemented as a 
replacement rate.4
Enchanted Rock’s microgrids and state-of-the-art gas generators provide continuous, 
dependable power supply to customers including manufacturing facilities, data centers, hospitals, 
water utilities, and other critical infrastructure.  Enchanted Rock submitted post-technical 
conference comments in AD24-11-0005 and appreciates the opportunity to further comment on 
co-location solutions to grid and resource adequacy challenges in PJM.   
As further described below, Enchanted Rock offers an additional option6 to facilitate co-
location arrangements, which Enchanted Rock refers to herein as the Load Co-located with 
Dispatchable Generation (“LCDG”) option.  Although the LCDG option is different than the 
New Options proposed by PJM, the LCDG option shares characteristics similar to New Options 
6 and 7.  Changes to the Tariff are necessary to effectuate the LCDG option and, therefore, 
Enchanted Rock respectfully submits that PJM’s existing Tariff is not just and reasonable.7
Enchanted Rock requests that the Commission issue an order directing replacement tariff 
provisions that allow customers in PJM to realize the benefits of LCDG as a co-location option.  
To the extent the Commission determines that further proceedings—either before the 
Commission, or as part of PJM’s stakeholder process—are needed before directing any changes 
to PJM’s Tariff, Enchanted Rock is committed to working collaboratively with PJM and 
stakeholders to develop such necessary changes to the Tariff.8
4 See Show Cause Order at Ordering Para (D).  
5 Post-Technical Conference Comments of Enchanted Rock, LLC, Docket No. AD24-11-000 (Dec. 9, 2024) (“Post-
Tech. Comments”). 
6 PJM presented eight existing or new co-location options (“New Options”).  See Answer of PJM Interconnection, 
L.L.C., Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al. (Mar. 24, 2025) (“PJM Answer”).  
7 In support of the LCDG option, Enchanted Rock presents the Affidavit of Dr. Albert W. Bremser, included 
herewith as Attachment A (“Bremser Affidavit”).  See Bremser Affidavit ¶¶ 9-20.  
8 Enchanted Rock, through its subsidiary Electranet REP I, LLC, is a member of PJM and participates through the 
Other Supplier sector.

3 
I.
INTRODUCTION AND NEED FOR REFORM 
The United States stands at the precipice of an unprecedented surge in electricity demand 
from large loads including data centers and large industrial and manufacturing facilities.9
Extraordinary load growth is fueled mostly by the proliferation of data centers that support 
artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and other services.  Over the next 15 years, PJM 
anticipates significant peak demand growth, with the summer peak rising by roughly 70 
gigawatts (“GW”), and the winter peak rising by roughly 65 GW.10  Enchanted Rock understands 
that securing a global competitive advantage in artificial intelligence is a U.S. priority and that 
maintaining data centers within U.S. borders is a critical national security interest.11  These 
extraordinary changes in demand require federal and state regulators, grid operators, market 
participants, and customers to pivot and look to innovations that optimize infrastructure without 
creating new reliability risks—particularly during periods when new generation capacity and 
transmission infrastructure is planned, permitted, and constructed.  The accelerating demand for 
electricity coupled with supply delays caused by lengthy permitting processes for generation and 
transmission infrastructure, as well as persistent supply chain delays for equipment, means the 
industry must devise immediately implementable solutions that optimize existing infrastructure 
and ensure that transmission expansion occurs in the most cost-effective way possible. 
9 See Large Loads Co-Located at General Facilities Technical Conference Transcript, Docket No. AD24-11-000, 
10:25 – 11:6 (Nov. 1, 2024) (“Technical Conf. Tr”) (Commissioner Christie stating “we’re seeing load forecasts 
shooting up . . . driven by data centers”). 
10 See Asim Z. Haque, Sr. Vice President – Governmental and Member Services, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 
Testimony before the U.S. House of Representatives, Committee on Energy & Commerce, Subcommittee on Energy 
(Mar. 5, 2025), available at: https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/library/reports-
notices/testimony/2025/20250305-haque-testimony-us-house-committee-on-energy-commerce.pdf. 
11 See Energy Subcommittee: “Scaling for Growth: Meeting the Demand for Reliable, Affordable Electricity” 
https://energycommerce.house.gov/events/energy-subcommittee-scaling-for-growth-meeting-the-demand-for-
reliable-affordable-electricity (Rep. Gary Palmer (R-AL) stating “My concern today is we’re in an arms race for 
artificial intelligence,” “And it’s clear we don’t have the capacity to build the data systems that we need in order to 
win that arms race with China.”).

4 
The Commission has already started work—issuing landmark rulemakings to improve the 
nation’s generator interconnection processes (via Order No. 202312), regional transmission 
planning and cost allocation processes (via Order No. 192013), siting interstate electric 
transmission facilities (via Order No. 197714), and increasing transmission capacity through 
ambient-adjusted transmission facility ratings (via Order No. 88115).  However, the full benefits 
of these rules have not yet been realized and will not be enough in the time horizon needed to 
support interconnection of, and service to, large loads.  Even with new procedures to secure 
needed generation capacity through surplus interconnection and expedited interconnection 
processes,16 PJM will still be challenged to meet the needs of rapidly growing demand, 
particularly for the artificial intelligence race. 
These challenges underscore the urgent need for innovative solutions.  A recent white 
paper from Duke University, entitled “Rethinking Load Growth,” published by the Nicholas 
Institute for Energy, Environment & Sustainability highlights that the U.S. power system has 
substantial headroom due to planning decisions to maintain reserves for infrequent peak demand 
events.17  By strategically curtailing their load during peak periods, flexible loads can tap into 
this existing headroom,18 allowing the grid to reliably and safely accommodate more load 
without requiring significant infrastructure upgrades.  According to the report, 98 GW of new 
12 See Improvements to Generator Interconnection Procedures and Agreements, Order No. 2023, 184 FERC ¶ 
61,054 (2023). 
13 See Building for the Future Through Electric Regional Transmission Planning and Cost Allocation, Order 
No.1920, 187 FERC ¶ 61,068, order on rehearing and clarification, Order No. 1920-A, 189 FERC ¶ 61,126 (2024). 
14 See Applications for Permits to Site Interstate Electric Transmission Facilities, Order No. 1977, 187 FERC ¶ 
61,069 (2024). 
15 See Managing Transmission Line Ratings, Order No. 881, 177 FERC ¶ 61,179 (2021). 
16 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,083 (2025); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,084 
(2025). 
17 See Tyler H. Norris, Tim Profeta, Dalia Patino-Echeverri, and Adam Cowie-Haskell, Rethinking Load Growth: 
Assessing the Potential for Integration of Large Flexible Loads in US Power Systems, Nicholas Institute for Energy, 
Environment & Sustainability (2025), available at: 
https://nicholasinstitute.duke.edu/sites/default/files/publications/rethinking-load-growth.pdf.  
18 See Bremser Affidavit ¶¶ 13-17.

5 
load—equivalent to more than 10% of the nation’s current aggregate peak demand—could be 
integrated at an average annual load curtailment rate of 0.5%, and 126 GW at a rate of 1.0%.19
In other words, the grid can accommodate a significant increase in demand if users are flexible 
and reduce their usage during system stress, which can occur during any time of the year, such as 
during the summer and winter peaks and during unplanned and planned transmission and 
generator outages in shoulder months. 
A risk exists that investments in new infrastructure responsive to the demand boom may, 
ultimately, be underutilized.20  Flexibility can hedge against this uncertainty by enabling a more 
gradual and adaptive approach to infrastructure development as a temporary measure until such 
time that new infrastructure can be built.  To bridge the timeline for construction of large-scale 
capacity expansion, flexible arrangements like the LCDG option can reduce demand during 
periods of system stress, whenever they may occur, in the interim.21  Enabling a temporary 
flexibility option that large loads can opt into would therefore mitigate some of these risks and 
allow for faster load interconnection.  Further, recognizing that load forecasting discussions 
around the country have coalesced around the need for greater transparency, Enchanted Rock 
believes that an opportunity exists for load forecasting practices to allow for greater granularity 
and to take into account more sophisticated concepts of flexibility, as the LCDG option would 
provide. 
19 See Tyler H. Norris, Tim Profeta, Dalia Patino-Echeverri, and Adam Cowie-Haskell, Rethinking Load Growth: 
Assessing the Potential for Integration of Large Flexible Loads in US Power Systems, Figure 1, Nicholas Institute 
for Energy, Environment & Sustainability (2025), available at: 
https://nicholasinstitute.duke.edu/sites/default/files/publications/rethinking-load-growth.pdf
20 See, e.g., PJM Answer at 66 (“With any forecast of future load growth, additional transmission and generation 
capacity may be required, and there is the risk of overbuilding due to a forecast that is too high, or underbuilding due 
to a forecast that is too low. The same is true with respect to large load additions, regardless of whether the load is 
co-located with generation. Given the potential size of these individual, large load additions that are in the forecast, 
uncertainty with respect to whether the large loads are actually added to the system could cause either overbuild or 
underbuild to occur based on a single customer addition.”). 
21 See Bremser Affidavit ¶¶ 18-19.

6 
As Commissioner Rosner recently recognized, flexibility is critical for addressing the 
rapid increase in the country’s electricity demand.22  As such, Enchanted Rock respectfully urges 
the Commission to direct changes to PJM’s Tariff to effectuate the LCDG option in order to 
facilitate large load flexibility in PJM.
II.
LCDG OPTION: LOAD CO-LOCATED WITH DISPATCHABLE GENERATION  
As PJM demonstrates in its answer, co-location may exist through a spectrum of different 
configurations.23  Enchanted Rock agrees.  At one end of the spectrum is what Enchanted Rock 
would describe as “Complete Electrical Isolation,” where the load and generation are entirely 
self-sufficient and islanded; at the other end is “Full Grid Integration,” with unrestricted power 
exchange with the grid, operating as a fully integrated load, using exclusively grid-sourced 
energy and capacity.  As shown below in Figure 1, between these two extremes (but closer to 
Full Grid Integration, as shown below) lies “Flexible Grid Integration,” which the LCDG option 
would facilitate.   
Figure 1 
22 See Technical Conf. Tr at 96:1-7 (Commissioner Rosner acknowledging the value of “flexibility of large load” 
given the “really rapid increase in demand”). 
23 See, e.g., PJM Answer, Exhibit A (Options for Service to Large Loads).

7 
Under Enchanted Rock’s view, Flexible Grid Integration is a co-location arrangement 
that relies on the PJM-operated transmission network for grid-sourced energy but provides 
flexibility commitments through dispatch of the customer’s co-located dispatchable generation 
during periods of system stress.  Flexible Grid Integration facilitates a system committed to grid-
sourced energy and regulated markets, integrates large loads into system planning, provides 
operational transparency into large loads, and enhances grid operator capabilities by giving large 
loads the opportunity to provide flexibility when grid operators need it. 
Enchanted Rock’s LCDG option, a type of Flexible Grid Integration, shares 
characteristics with PJM New Options 6 and 7, while also offering additional functionality.  The 
premise of the LCDG option is that load flexibility provides substantial benefits to a constrained 
system.  Load flexibility is key to accelerating large load interconnections and optimizing the 
efficient and cost-effective utilization of grid infrastructure.  Under the LCDG option, load and 
generation may be separately metered but are studied together for purposes of retail load 
interconnection and integration, transmission and resource adequacy planning, and operations.   
Table 1 below summarizes the key components of Enchanted Rock’s LCDG option, 
which is discussed in further detail herein.

8

The LCDG option applies to co-located load that takes Interruptible Service and Available

The LCDG option includes two-phases, providing an opportunity for load to bring-its-own 
generation when transmission or generation capacity on the system is not sufficient for full 
integration, thereby expediting interconnection and dispatch. 
During the waiting period for new transmission, or “Phase 1,” large load is treated as a non-
capacity backed load and avoids generation capacity costs in exchange for making firm 
commitments to support reliability in advance of emergency conditions via the dispatch of co-

during time periods when there is available transmission capacity.

The LCDG option provides more than a traditional demand response or peak shaving 
program during the operating period.  The flexibility provided by the LCDG option would be 
considered in the planning and study process for large load interconnection, local and regional 
planning, and resource adequacy.  The LCDG option therefore permits large loads to utilize 
flexibility to achieve faster interconnection through the deployment of dispatchable, co-located 
generation.  Under the LCDG option, the firm commitment to dispatch co-located generation 
would serve as a bridge to permanent grid upgrades for projects that would otherwise be delayed 
while new infrastructure is planned, permitted, and constructed.  
Specifically, under Phase 1 of Enchanted Rock’s proposal, LCDG load would be treated 
as curtailable non-Network Load, subscribing to Interruptible Service (as contemplated in PJM’s 
New Option 7) for generation service, and subscribing to Enchanted Rock’s proposed Available 
Transmission Capacity Service for transmission service.  Under Phase 1, LCDG generators 
would be classified as non-Network Resources (i.e., interconnected on a non-network basis), and 
would be limited to serving the co-located load’s main function of reducing or zeroing demand.25
Under Phase 2, LCDG load would be eligible to go through the normal PJM Tariff 
process as Network Load, when PJM deems that the supply/demand conditions are no longer 
constrained, and necessary transmission infrastructure (e.g., Network Upgrades) have been 
25 Additionally, during Phase 1, the Commission and PJM should allow the LCDG generators to participate in PJM’s 
wholesale markets and earn revenue for the services they are capable of providing consistent with the PJM Tariff.

10 
constructed and placed into service.  Unlike PJM’s New Option 6, LCDG load would not be 
Network Load, but would utilize Interruptible Service as a non-Network Load (i.e., for 
generation service) as contemplated in PJM’s New Option 7. 
Moreover, during Phase 1, the LCDG generator would act to curtail load (to the extent 
necessary).  Under Phase 2, LCDG generators would be eligible to go through the normal PJM 
Tariff process as a Network Resource and fast tracked through the generator interconnection 
process to the extent allowed by the Commission (e.g., consistent with PJM New Option 6).  
Notably, new load may be incentivized to self-supply generation if that generation were eligible 
to be fast-tracked in the generator interconnection process.   
Additionally, under Phase 1, Enchanted Rock proposes that projects choosing the LCDG 
option take a variation of non-firm transmission service to be called Available Transmission 
Capacity Service (“ATCS”),26 with commitments to dispatch co-located generation during PJM 
curtailments.  ATCS would be a transitional option available only until the transmission 
infrastructure is constructed and the utility is able to serve the load taking full network 
transmission service.  The proposed ATCS would allow load to access generation on the network 
during time periods when there is available transmission capacity.  Given the firm service nature 
of NITS, it would be appropriate to provide a new solution to unlock the unused capacity as 
interim transmission service for co-located arrangements.27
Similar to ERCOT’s “Connect and Manage” process for generation resources which 
expedites the interconnection of new generation resources by prioritizing local grid connections 
26 See Bremser Affidavit ¶¶ 6, 12-19
27 See id. ¶¶ 12-19.

11 
and managing broader system impacts in real-time operations,28 LCDG projects create a 
“Connect and Manage” option for large loads that make firm commitments to dispatch their co-
located generation.  During periods of grid stress in the waiting period, PJM operators would 
direct the dispatch available megawatts (“MWs”) of LCDG generation so that the LCDG load 
reduces electricity consumption from the grid.  In the event LCDG generation fails to respond to 
dispatch instructions, the LCDG load would need to be curtailed to provide the requested 
response.   
Enchanted Rock expects that LCDG generation would be dispatched only for a small 
number of hours per year.  As shown below in Figure 2, a typical load duration curve (the blue 
line) reflects the entire annual hourly load for 8760 hours.  The orange line represents a 
hypothetical addition of X MWs from data centers.  Data centers typically have baseload 
computing needs and exceptionally high load factors29 due to their high uptime requirements 
necessary to align with customer needs,30 meaning that the applicable curve will just shift 
upwards by that amount.

Generation-Entity-Winter-Weather-Preparedness-Fernandes.pdf.

Here-to-Stay-but-Are-Data-Centers-2.pdf. 
30 See The Data Center, The Importance of Uptime in the Data Center (Sept. 11, 2019), available at:

In this way, LCDG projects would support efficient utilization of existing generation and 
transmission capacity, lowering costs for customers of the existing transmission system, and 
buying time for new infrastructure necessary to serve the load on a firm basis to be placed in

13 
III.
ENCHANTED ROCK’S RESPONSE TO SELECTED COMMISSION 
QUESTIONS 
a. General 
iv. Parties may also address how co-located loads are similar to or disparate 
from other types of arrangements where load and generation share the same 
point of interconnection (such as Behind the Meter Generation as defined in 
PJM’s Tariff or non-retail behind the meter generation). 
Enchanted Rock’s Response: 
Unlike LCDG, the Behind the Meter Generation (“BTMG”) construct assumes 
continuous supply if the load cannot draw from the transmission network, whereas a more 
flexible solution would allow for periodic supply to load but continued access to the transmission 
network during normal operating conditions.  BTMG assets can reduce customers’ capacity and 
transmission demand payments via full netting of the load, whereas LCDG projects temporarily 
relieve constraints on existing infrastructure allowing for immediate utilization of idle or 
underutilized transmission capacity for faster load interconnections. 
d. Interconnection Procedures and Cost Allocation 
ii. Please explain whether PJM’s necessary study process allows a colocation 
arrangement to demonstrate its capability to flexibly adjust its withdrawals 
from or injections to the transmission system (e.g., by using secondary 
backup generation or by curtailing on-site load), and reflect this capability in 
the operating assumptions PJM considers when estimating the co-location 
arrangement’s impacts on the transmission system?  If not, would it be 
appropriate to establish a new or revised study process that allows for such a 
demonstration? 
Enchanted Rock’s Response: 
Currently, load and generation interconnection requests are studied separately.  This 
disjointed approach creates several issues, particularly for co-located arrangements where the 
load and generation components are intended to function as an integrated system.  First, it can 
lead to a mismatch in timing.  The generation and load portions of a co-located arrangement may

14 
face different timelines for interconnection, making it challenging to bring the entire facility 
online in a coordinated manner.  This mismatch in study timelines can delay project completion 
and create bottlenecks, as project timelines become constrained by the interconnection study 
process with the longest duration.  
Second, separate studies fail to account for the interdependencies between the load and 
generation components of a co-located arrangement.  When studies are conducted independently, 
the load interconnection study may not consider the impact of the co-located generation, and vice 
versa.  This can result in inaccurate assessments of the necessary transmission upgrades and can 
lead to inefficient interconnection solutions.  
Recognizing and respecting jurisdictional boundaries between load and generator 
interconnections, Enchanted Rock recommends improving coordination so that grid planners in 
multiple jurisdictions can gain a more accurate understanding of the co-located arrangement’s 
overall impact on the grid.  For example, by enabling the generation component to offset some of 
the load’s impact on the grid, it may defer the need for certain upgrades for reliable 
interconnection until such time that infrastructure expansion can occur.  Consideration for co-
located arrangements in the retail load integration process would also allow for faster load 
interconnections and mitigates commercial risks for both load and generation developers.  
Facilitating improved coordination aligns with the response to the Show Cause Order of certain 
indicated transmission owners in PJM, which transmission owners also emphasized the need to 
value load flexibility in the overall planning process.31
31 See Answer of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al., Attachment A at 13 
(Mar. 24, 2025).

15 
vii. Please explain whether changes to interconnection procedures and 
agreements are necessary to accommodate new generation interconnecting 
with co-located load, including whether the existing queue process is 
sufficient for such arrangements. 
Enchanted Rock’s Response: 
PJM’s interconnection procedures were developed for generation-only projects, not co-
located arrangements, which by their nature, integrate generation and load to function as a 
unified resource, yet the separate processes fail to recognize this fundamental characteristic.  
This separation manifests in several critical ways within the interconnection process: 
·
Uncoordinated Studies: the generation interconnection study (mainly FERC-
jurisdictional) and the load interconnection study (mainly state-jurisdictional) are 
frequently conducted independently, without proper consideration of co-located 
arrangements’ combined impact. 
·
Timing Mismatches: the separate processes can result in different timelines for 
interconnecting generation and load at co-located arrangements. This can create 
significant delays and logistical hurdles for co-located projects.  
·
Inadequate Agreements: existing interconnection agreements are generally designed for 
either standalone generation facilities or standalone loads and may not contain the 
necessary provisions to address the unique operational arrangements of co-located 
facilities. 
·
Queue Management: generator interconnection study processes and queues may not 
adequately recognize the benefits that co-located arrangements can provide and may 
require reforms to prioritize the grid flexibility benefits offered by co-located 
arrangements, like LCDG projects. 
Moreover, to the extent that the Commission orders an accelerated interconnection 
process consistent with PJM’s proposed Option 6, LCDG projects should also be permitted to 
participate in any accelerated interconnection process for any generation co-located with load.  
Facilitating the integration of LCDG projects will incentivize the development of resources that 
align with grid needs.

16 
f.  Other 
ii. Please discuss whether back-up service can provide benefits to customers 
or otherwise help minimize system costs, including with specific examples or 
best practices, if possible. 
Enchanted Rock’s Response: 
Backup generators can indeed provide benefits to customers and help minimize system 
costs.  Large loads, like data centers, may already have capital and ongoing expenses earmarked 
for backup generation to maintain operational continuity during disruptions of their primary 
power source as a matter of normal planning.  In PJM’s Option 8, PJM appears to suggest that 
the easing of existing restrictions, such as EPA’s National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air 
Pollutants (NESHAP), particularly for Tier 2 diesel generators, could be low hanging fruit to add 
to the supply stack as grid servicing assets via demand response. 
However, the proposition to relax environmental constraints on Tier 2 diesel generators 
warrants careful scrutiny.  While such a measure may appear to offer increased flexibility in grid 
management and demand response, it is ultimately unnecessary and potentially 
counterproductive, given the readily available and cost-competitive cleaner alternatives.  Natural 
gas generators, for example, present a superior emissions profile,32 yielding lower levels of 
particulate matter (PM), sulfur oxides (SOX), and nitrogen oxides (NOX).  Additionally, diesel 
generators carry risks related to fuel availability and delivery, especially after widespread 
outages when a surge in demand from numerous diesel users simultaneously attempting to refuel 
GWs of backup generation capacity can quickly overwhelm supply chains. 
While the relaxation of environmental limits on Tier 2 diesel generators may offer a 
seemingly expedient solution for valuing backup power in the supply stack, the adoption of 
32 Enchanted Rock Fact Sheet (last visited April 23, 2025), available at: https://enchantedrock.com/enchanted-rock-
fact-sheet/.

17 
Enchanted Rock’s proposed LCDG option would encourage large loads to adopt commercially 
available generation technologies that can improve flexibility on the grid and ultimately provide 
resource adequacy value to the grid without special environmental waivers. 
iii. Parties may also choose to address how co-location arrangements may 
provide benefits, including potentially reducing required transmission 
upgrades to interconnect large loads, reducing congestion, or providing   
operational flexibility during system peaks or emergencies. 
Enchanted Rock’s Response: 
Co-location arrangements, particularly those involving LCDG, can provide several 
benefits to the grid and its operation.  By deploying dispatchable co-located generation, a large 
load can effectively become an interruptible load.  If this capability is valued in the transmission 
planning process before load interconnection, it may allow grid planners to defer the need for 
certain transmission upgrades that would otherwise be required to serve the new load.  The co-
located generation can be used to offset the load’s impact on the grid during peak demand and 
stress periods.  
In PJM utility territories that rely heavily on centralized transmission and lack sufficient 
local generation, co-location arrangements can help reduce congestion and backfill any required 
transmission contingencies in the interim as new transmission is built to solve the violations.  In 
most cases, these co-located arrangements can even be configured to export excess generation to 
the grid because normal industry practice is to oversize backup generation for redundancy 
purposes. This capability helps to stabilize the grid, avert blackouts, and optimize the utilization 
of existing grid infrastructure. 
Co-location also contributes to improve overall system efficiency by reducing 
transmission line losses, which represent a not insignificant portion of the total electricity

18 
generated, with some amount lost between the generation source and the end-use customer.33
The amount of energy lost is dependent on factors such as the distance the electricity travels, the 
characteristics of the transmission lines, and the level of current flowing through the lines.  By 
locating generation sources closer to load, co-location arrangements minimize the distance that 
electricity needs to travel across the transmission network.  Lower transmission losses mean that 
less electricity needs to be generated to serve the same amount of load, freeing up capacity on 
existing transmission infrastructure for use by other customers. 
iv. Parties may also address whether, and if so, how, the Tariff should be 
modified to best accommodate or encourage co-location arrangements to be 
constructed in such a way as to minimize total system costs or otherwise 
provide certain benefits, including protections for existing customers and    
allocation of costs consistent with the cost-causation principle. 
Enchanted Rock’s Response: 
For the reasons described herein, Enchanted Rock respectfully submits that the PJM 
Tariff should be modified to adopt Enchanted Rock’s LCDG option as outlined above, including 
the proposed Available Transmission Capacity Service.34  Enchanted Rock’s proposed LCDG 
option would encourage co-location of dispatchable generation with new loads at a time when 
resource adequacy is being challenged and markets are expecting to continue to deal with thin 
reserve margins going forward.  In essence, a combination of PJM’s New Option 6 and New 
Option 7, with additional transmission-related considerations, would enable LCDG projects to 
provide their full value to the grid.

III.REASONS TO UPDATE THE PJM TARIFF (POTENTIAL ISSUES WITH THE 
CURRENT PJM TARIFF) 
9. Co-located arrangements with new generation and new large loads are differently 
situated than a point of interconnection involving only generation or only load.  Further, 
co-located arrangements with new generation and new large loads are distinguishable 
from proposed co-location arrangements where there is a pre-existing relationship with 
PJM involving assets with current and continuing operations.  For example, with 
existing generation, the PJM transmission system was likely modified to accommodate 
that generation.  
10. Updating the PJM Tariff to accommodate co-located arrangements with new 
generation and new large loads would align with removing impediments to competition 
in the PJM wholesale power markets to serve large loads.  This would align with a 
fundamental principle of Order No. 888 in promoting competition and efficiency.2
11. Updating the PJM Tariff will help avoid undue discrimination and will help allow open 
access to the PJM transmission system to co-located arrangements with new generation 
and new large loads.
